title: The dangers of cyberloafing “
paragraphs: Time to own up. When you‘re sitting at your computer, do you work solidly all day? Or do you allow yourself to become distracted now and again... to open a few extra tabs, check social media, read a spot of news, browse the latest fashion trends, maybe catch up on some celebrity gossip, and look at some...

Stop! You’re ’cyberloafing‘. The unwieldy word is a combination of ’cyber‘, which means ’related to computers‘, and ’loafing‘, which means ’relaxing in a lazy way‘. We do it, and we do it a lot. A study from the University of Texas suggests we are guilty of this form of procrastination for 14% of our working day. On a Friday afternoon, I expect it’s more than that.
I‘ll admit to indulging in the odd bout of cyberloafing myself. In fact I’ve already done it in the course of writing this story. OK, more than once.

But it‘s a slippery slope. It can damage your productivity and even your career. Because according to the Univeristy of Texas research, each time a worker gets sidetracked by the internet it takes an average of 23 minutes to get back to work.

More than that, cyberloafing has a dark side, according to a report published in The Journal of Psychosocial Research on Cyberspace. It argues that cyberloafing is connected to several negative personality traits. People who cyberloaf are more likely to be manipulative, self-interested and narcissistic. Furthermore, people with these traits are less likely to feel remorse about avoiding work, and less concerned about getting caught.

Why do we do it? For some, it’s undoubtedly an escape from the drudgery of what they‘re supposed to be doing. Or a way of avoiding tackling that ever growing in-tray. Some might get a feeling of satisfaction, get a buzz from finding a great deal online. But overall, it’s something that takes you away from what you‘re actually being paid to do, or paying to do: if you’re a student.

When you have the whole world of the internet at your fingertips, it‘s hard to resist. How do we nip it in the bud? If you can truly ask yourself why you are cyberloafing, then that can help identify the base problem. And if that sounds like too much hard work, you could just switch off the internet for a couple of hours!
So in the meantime, let me just close those extra tabs...

vocabulary.entry: distracted [adj.] /dɪˈstræktɪd/ 分心的；注意力不集中的
vocabulary.example: He was distracted by the noise and couldn‘t focus.
vocabulary.translation: 他被噪音分了心，无法集中注意力。

vocabulary.entry: cyberloafing [n.] /ˈsaɪbəˌləʊfɪŋ/ 网络摸鱼（在工作时间利用网络做与工作无关的事情）(新词；口语)
vocabulary.example: Cyberloafing is a common problem in modern offices.
vocabulary.translation: 网络摸鱼是现代办公室里的常见问题。

vocabulary.entry: procrastination [n.] /prəˌkræstɪˈneɪʃən/ 拖延；耽搁 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: Procrastination can lead to missed deadlines.
vocabulary.translation: 拖延可能导致错过截止日期。

vocabulary.entry: indulging in [phr.] /ɪnˈdʌldʒɪŋ ɪn/ 沉迷于；沉溺于
vocabulary.example: He spends his weekends indulging in his hobbies.
vocabulary.translation: 他周末沉浸在爱好中。

vocabulary.entry: slippery slope [n.] /ˌslɪpəri ˈsləʊp/ 滑坡效应；越来越糟的情况
vocabulary.example: Missing one deadline can be a slippery slope.
vocabulary.translation: 错过一次截止日期可能会引发越来越糟的情况。

vocabulary.entry: sidetracked [adj.] /ˈsaɪdtrækt/ 分心的；转移目标的 (口语)
vocabulary.example: I got sidetracked by a phone call and forgot what I was doing.
vocabulary.translation: 我被一个电话分了心，忘了自己在做什么。

vocabulary.entry: manipulative [adj.] /məˈnɪpjʊlətɪv/ 善于操控的；有控制欲的 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: She has a manipulative personality and always gets her way.
vocabulary.translation: 她有操控欲的性格，总能达到自己的目的。

vocabulary.entry: self-interested [adj.] /ˌself ˈɪntrəstɪd/ 自私的；利己的 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: His actions were purely self-interested.
vocabulary.translation: 他的行为纯粹是自私自利的。

vocabulary.entry: narcissistic [adj.] /ˌnɑːsɪˈsɪstɪk/ 自恋的；自我陶醉的 (心理学词汇)
vocabulary.example: Narcissistic people often lack empathy for others.
vocabulary.translation: 自恋的人常常缺乏对他人的共情。

vocabulary.entry: remorse [n.] /rɪˈmɔːs/ 懊悔；悔恨 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: He felt no remorse for his actions.
vocabulary.translation: 他对自己的行为毫无悔意。

vocabulary.entry: drudgery [n.] /ˈdrʌdʒəri/ 苦差事；繁重无聊的工作 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: The drudgery of data entry bored him.
vocabulary.translation: 数据录入的枯燥工作让他厌烦。

vocabulary.entry: buzz [n.] /bʌz/ 兴奋感；快感 (口语)
vocabulary.example: Winning the competition gave him a real buzz.
vocabulary.translation: 赢得比赛给了他很大的兴奋感。

vocabulary.entry: nip it in the bud [phr.] /nɪp ɪt ɪn ðə bʌd/ 防患于未然；把……消灭在萌芽状态
vocabulary.example: We need to nip this problem in the bud before it gets worse.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要在这个问题恶化之前就防患于未然。

vocabulary.entry: unwieldy [adj.] /ʌnˈwiːldi/ 笨拙的；难操作的；拗口的
vocabulary.example: The word ‘cyberloafing’ is a bit unwieldy.
vocabulary.translation: “cyberloafing”这个词有点拗口。

vocabulary.entry: productivity [n.] /ˌprɒdʌkˈtɪvəti/ 生产力；生产效率
vocabulary.example: Taking regular breaks can improve productivity.
vocabulary.translation: 定期休息可以提高生产力。

vocabulary.entry: tackling [v.] /ˈtæklɪŋ/ 处理；解决 (原形: tackle)
vocabulary.example: The government is tackling the issue of homelessness.
vocabulary.translation: 政府正在解决无家可归的问题。

vocabulary.entry: in-tray [n.] /ˈɪn treɪ/ 收文盘；待处理文件盘 (英式英语)
vocabulary.example: My in-tray is full of documents that need attention.
vocabulary.translation: 我的收文盘里满是需要处理的文件。

vocabulary.entry: fingertips [n. pl.] /ˈfɪŋɡətɪps/ 指尖；at one‘s fingertips 触手可及

vocabulary.translation: 有了互联网，信息触手可及。

vocabulary.entry: identify [v.] /aɪˈdentɪfaɪ/ 识别；确定

vocabulary.translation: 你能认出这张照片里的人吗？

vocabulary.entry: base [adj.] /beɪs/ 根本的；基础的
vocabulary.example: We need to address the base cause of the problem.
vocabulary.translation: 我们需要解决问题的根本原因。
